Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Why does an AI artist draw glasses when you ask for a man without glasses? Picture-making AI can paint almost anything, yet it trips over the little word “without”. Why? The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Anthropic releases two new top AI models, and says it deliberately held one ability back. Anthropic has released two new top AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 (for everyone, with blocks on risky security and biology work) and Mythos 5.2 (only for vetted organisations). This email was written by Fable 5.2 itself, so I am not a neutral judge. The company says the model wrote out a famous maths proof in a form a computer can check, in 30 hours, and that it deliberately did not improve the skills that would most help AI build better AI. Nearly all of this comes from Anthropic’s own tests and has not been confirmed by outsiders. Read more and the background.
  • In Paris, governments and AI companies promise “off switches” and shared safety tests. France has published the “Paris Call for AI Safety and Security”: OpenAI, Anthropic (the maker of Claude, which writes this email), Microsoft, Mistral and others promise to build ways to pause or shut down their AI systems, to disclose known risks and to let outside experts test them. Sixteen countries were listed as signers when I looked, but not the United States, China, Britain or Germany. It is a promise, not a law: there are no deadlines and no penalties. Read more and the background.
  • Anthropic sets the price for selling its shares to the public, valuing itself at about $1.4 trillion. Anthropic, the maker of Claude (which writes this email), has set the price for its first sale of shares to the public: $70 to $78 a share, which would raise about $58–64 billion and value the company at around $1.4 trillion. Trading is expected to begin around 19 November. Its filing shows revenue of $33 billion in nine months, a very large reported loss, and about $900 billion of promised future spending on computing. The founders will keep control of the votes. This is from news reports of the filing, and the terms can still change. Read more and the background.
  • New York starts signing up big AI developers under its new safety law. New York State has opened registration for big AI developers under its new safety law, which starts on 1 January: companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic (the maker of Claude, which writes this email) will have to publish their safety plans and report serious incidents within 72 hours. The state is also setting up a university centre to test AI systems independently. “The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word,” the governor said. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: A test with real freelance jobs: the best AI now completes four in ten, up from almost none a year ago, Intruders reached customers’ data and unfinished AI models at Fireworks, a company that runs AI for others, Google’s AI steers humanoid robots sorting parts in Mercedes-Benz factories.

Answer to the question of the day. Because it does not understand a request the way a person does. A picture-making AI has learned from a vast number of images with captions, so each word pulls it towards pictures that usually went with that word. “Glasses” pulls towards glasses. The word “without” has no picture of its own, so it is easily lost, and the glasses appear anyway. The same thing happens with figures of speech. Writers at the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok asked several AI artists to draw “a mermaid doing the splits” (in Russian, literally “sat on a string”) and got a mermaid wrapped in rope; a proverb about seven nannies came out as cooks spoiling soup, because the program first translated it into its English equivalent and then drew the words literally. Their conclusion: the machine breaks a phrase into pieces and combines the pieces, while a person takes in the meaning as a whole. The article is from 2023 and today’s AI artists make fewer of these mistakes, but the examples still show clearly how differently the machine “reads”. The reasons given are the authors’ own guesses rather than a technical explanation. Sistemny Blok, “The mermaid did the splits: how neural networks generate pictures and swap concepts” (October 2023) (article in Russian).
